item.title: EvoSurv: Evolution-Aware Multimodal Survival Modeling Reveals Complementary Prognostic Signals
item.description: arXiv:2611.13190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate cancer survival prediction remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Although multimodal survival models integrate clinical and molecular data, they often overlook evolutionary information encoded in genomic alterations. To address this gap, we developed eTime, a 38-dimensional evolutionary representation comprising eight feature groups that characterize clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, functional consequences, copy-number alterations, and anoikis-related genomic changes. We further developed EvoSurv, a multimodal survival framework integrating eTime with clinical variables and RNA expression. Across six TCGA cancer cohorts comprising 2,782 patients, EvoSurv achieved the highest mean concordance index (C-index) in all six cancers, averaging 0.663 and outperforming three state-of-the-art survival prediction methods. More importantly, we assessed whether evolutionary features provide additional prognostic information beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors. eTime remained significantly associated with survival in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) after adjustment for clinical variables and RNA-derived risk scores. Feature-group analyses further revealed cancer-specific prognostic patterns. In HNSC, T>G substitutions were associated with increased mortality risk after clinical and molecular adjustment, including in HPV-negative patients, with supporting evidence from an independent CPTAC-HNSCC cohort. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eTime captures survival-associated evolutionary information and highlight its potential to provide prognostic value beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors.
item.dc:creator: Wei Wang, Po-Yu Liang, Jun Bai

item.title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.13398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.
item.dc:creator: Maria Franz, N. Benjamin Erichson

item.title: Benchmarking large language models for parameter-level structural identifiability classification in epidemic ODE models
item.description: arXiv:2611.14184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural identifiability determines whether unknown parameters can be uniquely recovered from ideal model outputs, making it a prerequisite for interpreting parameter estimates. We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably provide preliminary structural identifiability classifications for epidemic models. We constructed a retrospective benchmark of 88 scenarios from 14 of the 27 studies considered, encompassing 696 parameter-level formal reference classifications from published results or Julia-based symbolic analysis. Scenarios were evaluated using Domain-Aware and canonically relabeled ("Domain-Anonymized") prompts, with ten runs per configuration and prompt condition. Six configurations completed all scheduled responses, yielding 83,520 parameter-level decisions for the primary comparison. GPT-5.5 Instant and GPT-5.5 Thinking Medium had the highest accuracies among complete configurations (88.71% and 88.07%). Canonical relabeling improved both configurations and attenuated their performance decline in scenarios with many unknown parameters or state variables, although effects differed across model families. Locally identifiable parameters were the most difficult class (highest strict recall among complete configurations: 42.00%), although the local reference set was small. In multivariable analysis, each additional unknown parameter reduced the odds of correct classification (OR 0.881; 95% CI 0.852-0.910), whereas additional observed outputs increased them (OR 1.666; 95% CI 1.503-1.846). Exploratory evaluations indicated strong performance for GPT-5.5 Thinking High and Claude Opus 5, despite incomplete coverage. LLMs may generate preliminary hypotheses or flag cases for formal review, provided outputs are checked against published results or formal symbolic methods. They should not be used to certify the structural identifiability of a complete model.
item.dc:creator: Geunsoo Jang, K. Sel\c{c}uk Candan, Gerardo Chowell

item.title: Pulsatile Endocrine Regulation with a Releasable Hormone Pool: Impulsive Feedback Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.13277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An impulsive model of endocrine regulation equipped with frequency- and amplitude-modulated pulsatile feedback is extended to study the dynamical effects pertaining to limitations due to the releasable hormone pool. The model describes a three-hormone regulatory loop and is applicable to endocrine systems such as the reproductive, stress, and growth hormone axes. Conditions guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of a periodic solution with a single feedback-triggered impulse per period (a 1-cycle) are derived, together with monotonicity properties of its characteristics. An explicit Jacobian formula is obtained to assess local orbital stability. Model analysis demonstrates that a reduced hormone-pool replenishment rate produces a lower-amplitude, higher-frequency 1-cycle. This behavior is consistent with experimentally observed alterations in testosterone regulation in aging human males.
item.dc:creator: Anton V. Proskurnikov, Alexander Medvedev

item.title: Similar visual tuning conceals different recovery dynamics in a model of macaque V1
item.description: arXiv:2611.13692v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biologically detailed neuronal networks can model how brain circuits perform observed functions, but their high computational cost limits the comparisons needed to test biological hypotheses. To address this limitation, we extend a multiscale approach in which responses of small populations of spiking neurons are computed in advance and reused across a larger cortical circuit. In particular, we approximate these local responses by deep neural networks and achieve an estimated acceleration of the order $10^5$ for steady-state evaluation relative to spiking network simulation. Beyond computational acceleration, the smooth deep surrogate of local responses provides derivatives, allowing us to analyze linear stability and to trace how a perturbation in brain activity is transmitted through different pathways. We demonstrate the approach in a model of an input layer of macaque primary visual cortex (V1), testing circuits under visual stimulation and controlled perturbations. We resolve pathway contributions to stability, strong recurrent responses, and slow recovery. Yet different combinations of pathway strengths can support similar responses to visual stimuli while producing different recovery dynamics. Therefore, Steady responses and perturbation recovery place complementary constraints on candidate circuits. Overall, our approach offers efficient evaluation with an interpretable circuit structure, making systematic comparisons across stimuli and biological hypotheses practical.
item.dc:creator: Xialei Huang, Qingyu Yan, Zheng Bian, Zhuo-Cheng Xiao

item.title: Influence of the branching geometry on SPION propagation: coupling of experiment and simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.13876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Magnetic Drug Targeting (MDT) is an emerging therapeutic concept in cancer medicine, where superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) are used as carriers for medication. Their magnetic properties allow for the manipulation of particle transport within the vascular structure and thus targeted delivery to the tumor site. To develop effective concepts for particle steering and accumulation, a detailed understanding of the particle--flow interaction, especially at asymmetric vascular bifurcations, is needed. Based on hierarchical scaling laws, generalized bifurcation geometries with varying degrees of asymmetry were derived and additively manufactured. The particle distribution was investigated by in situ optical measurements under different flow conditions and magnetic field configurations and compared with Lagrangian particle and Volume of Fluid Simulations (VoFS). While the particle mass partition followed the hydraulic flow split in asymmetric bifurcations, density-driven stratification dominated in the symmetric bifurcation, where one daughter branch received only a minor fraction of the particle mass at low flow rates despite carrying half of the flow. The Lagrangian model reproduced the predominantly advective propagation, whereas only the VoFS approach captured the stratification-induced asymmetry. Magnetic actuation counteracted the stratification, reversed the passive branch preference and increased particle retention. From a molecular communication perspective, bifurcation geometry, collective volume effects and magnetic actuation thus jointly determine the received particle signal at vascular bifurcations.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Fleischhauer, Luiz C. P. Wille, Stefan Lyer, Jens Kirchner, Dietmar Drummer

item.title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.14511v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.
item.dc:creator: Megha Srivastava, Michael H. Lim, Allison M. Keys, Pranav Murugan, Nate Gruver

item.title: Learning Deep Phylogeny Through Epistasis-Aware Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2604.22997v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Epistasis shapes protein evolution because the effect of a substitution depends on its sequence background. Site-independent substitution models can recover phylogeny accurately, but their resolution declines as substitutions accumulate and reshape mutational constraints. Potts models describe family-specific epistatic landscapes but leave the histories traversed through them unresolved. We introduce a generative framework that learns family-specific evolutionary structure directly from sequences evolving on such landscapes. Our variational autoencoder uses a covariance-matching loss to target epistatic dependencies and a correlation loss to align latent distance with sequence divergence before p-distance saturates. We compare two implementations that differ only in latent geometry. EucEvoGen uses Euclidean space, and HyperEvoGen uses a Poincar\'e ball. Trained on natural protein alignments, both reproduce family-level sequence diversity and recover higher-order sequence statistics beyond pairwise marginals more accurately than a Potts-model generator. In simulations of sequence evolution along Yule trees under a Potts Hamiltonian, HyperEvoGen recovers the known topologies at least as accurately as maximum-likelihood inference, improving on it for four of five tree-distance metrics. Its ancestral sequence reconstructions trail maximum likelihood for closely related sequences, overtake it beyond roughly 0.3 p-distance, and retain that advantage as divergence increases. EucEvoGen matches HyperEvoGen in sequence generation but yields less accurate phylogenetic inference. This comparison links the accuracy of deep phylogenetic inference to the global organization of the latent space. These results suggest that family-specific representations of epistatically constrained sequence space can extend phylogenetic inference into the regime where stationary site-independent models lose resolution.
item.dc:creator: Jason Lamanna, Erfan Mowlaei, Xinghua Shi, Sudhir Kumar, Vincenzo Carnevale

item.title: Reconstruction quality and restart repeatability are insufficient indicators of muscle synergy recovery by nonnegative matrix factorisation
item.description: arXiv:2609.21394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Muscle-synergy studies use factorisation methods such as nonnegative matrix factorisation (NMF) to extract muscle synergies from surface electromyography (sEMG). Reconstruction quality and restart repeatability are commonly used to evaluate these estimates, but whether they indicate recovery of underlying synergies remains unclear. Here, we defined synergy recovery as selection of the correct ground-truth rank and a minimum matched spatial cosine similarity of at least 0.80. We generated 4320 independent 16-muscle sEMG sequences across five simulation factors: ground-truth rank, signal-to-noise ratio, sequence length, spatial mixing and activation mixing. Rank selection used a variance accounted for (VAF) threshold of 0.90. At the selected ranks, NMF achieved VAF of at least 0.90 for every sequence, with median restart repeatability of 0.985. However, synergy recovery was achieved in only 7.92% of sequences. Supplying the ground-truth rank increased recovery to 60.79%. Reconstruction quality and restart repeatability had modest associations with spatial cosine similarity (Spearman's rho = 0.253 and 0.281, respectively). Recovery varied with all five factors, with nine significant two-factor interactions in exploratory analyses. In a supporting analysis, we assessed recovery using reference signals constructed from spatial weights and activation coefficients estimated from measured sEMG during five movement conditions. Selected ranks were lower than reference ranks in all five conditions despite high reconstruction quality. Accurate reconstruction and repeatable estimates therefore did not establish recovery of the underlying synergy structure. Physiological interpretations require additional evidence of functional relevance and assessment of sensitivity to the selected rank.
item.dc:creator: Ye Ma, Dongwei Liu, Meijin Hou, Chenyi Guo

item.title: A Bayesian approach to model uncertainty in single-cell genomic data
item.description: arXiv:2508.02061v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Network models provide a powerful framework for analysing single-cell count data, facilitating the characterisation of cellular identities, disease mechanisms, and developmental trajectories. However, uncertainty modeling in unsupervised learning with genomic data remains insufficiently explored. Conventional clustering methods assign a singular identity to each cell, potentially obscuring transitional states during differentiation or mutation. This study introduces a variational Bayesian framework for clustering and analysing single-cell genomic data, employing a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model with Dirichlet priors to estimate the probabilistic association of cells with distinct clusters. This approach captures cellular transitions, yielding biologically coherent insights into neurogenesis and breast cancer progression. The inferred clustering probabilities enable further analyses, including Differential Expression Analysis and pseudotime analysis. We propose the Area Under the Curve as a novel way of quantifying clustering performance in relation to cell-type specific marker genes, as it better captures the clustering characteristics of interest and aligns closely with visual assessments in the scRNA-seq data. To summarise, this methodological advancement enhances the resolution of single-cell data analysis, enabling a more nuanced characterisation of dynamic cellular identities in development and disease.
item.dc:creator: Shanshan Ren, Thomas E. Bartlett, Lina Gerontogianni, Swati Chandna

item.title: DiffeoMorph: Learning Distributed 3D Morphogenesis with Rotation-Invariant Spectral Shape Matching
item.description: arXiv:2512.17129v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Biological systems can form complex three-dimensional structures through the collective behavior of agents that share a common update rule and operate without central control. How such distributed control gives rise to precise global patterns remains a central question not only in developmental biology but also in distributed robotics, programmable matter, and multi-agent learning. Here, we introduce DiffeoMorph, an end-to-end differentiable framework for learning a morphogenesis protocol that guides a population of agents to morph into a target 3D shape. Each agent updates its position and internal state using an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network, based on its own internal state and signals received from other agents. To train this system, we introduce a new shape-matching loss based on 3D Zernike polynomials, which compares the predicted and target shapes as continuous spatial distributions, not as discrete point clouds, and is invariant to agent ordering, number of agents, and global orientation. To achieve rotation invariance while preserving reflection sensitivity, we include an alignment step that optimally rotates the predicted Zernike spectrum to match the target before computing the loss. We perform benchmarking to establish the advantages of our shape-matching loss over other standard distance metrics for shape comparison tasks. We then demonstrate that DiffeoMorph can form a range of complex shapes from minimally patterned initial conditions. DiffeoMorph provides a general framework for learning distributed control strategies for morphogenesis, swarm robotics, and programmable self-assembly.
item.dc:creator: Seong Ho Pahng, Guoye Guan, Benjamin Fefferman, Sahand Hormoz

item.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.01666v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. Taking biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used. A second failure arises whenever many sites share one action sequence, as in world models: the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from -17.3 to -6832 as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E = 1.1e10). Every single tempering factor we tried, estimated from residuals or tuned on validation data, collapsed in some setting; mixtures over a fixed grid of factors never did. In registered tests on three world-model families trained by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units of a diffusion model in which actions mattered, and reached the registered power bar in 10 of 26 Atari games under IRIS's own token likelihood and 1 of 6 control tasks under TD-MPC2; mixtures fixed in advance reached it in all 96 units, 24 of 26 games and 6 of 6 tasks. Under exact nulls the statistics made 4 rejections in 22,848 tests.
item.dc:creator: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen, Jiaying Li
